newsitem.title: USA: Merck compound reduces heart risks-studies.
newsitem.headline: Merck compound reduces heart risks-studies.

text.p: Aggrastat, a compound under development by Merck & Co Inc, was shown in two studies released Monday to reduce the risks of heart attack and other cardiac problems when used in combination with other drugs in patients with unstable angina.

"We believe with this drug that we prevented platelet thrombus formation ... This is like a cure of the unstable angina state," said Dr. Pierre Theroux of the Montreal Heart Institute, which conducted the 1,900-patient PRISM-Plus study using Aggrastat in combination with aspirin and heparin.
Heart attack risk was cut by 47 percent after seven days in patients suffering from unstable angina, said the Montreal study released here during an American College of Cardiology conference.

Unstable angina is a transitional condition between stable angina, in which arteries in the heart are partially blocked, and possible heart attack in which a section of the heart dies due to obstructed blood flow.
Reductions were also shown in the PRISM-Plus study for risks of death and reduced blood flow to the heart muscle, the researchers reported.
Other drugs on the market working in ways similar to the Merck compound include ReoPro, from Centocor Inc and Eli Lilly & Co.

PRISM, a separate study involving 3,200 patients in two groups, tested Aggrastat alone against heparin, a widely used blood-thinning medication. Both groups of patients received aspirin, a standard therapy for thinning blood.
After 48 hours, combined risk of death, heart attack and obstructed blood flow was lowered by 36 percent, the study found.

"The results of the PRISM study mirrored reductions in heart attack and death seen in the PRISM-Plus study ... Taken together, in these studies Aggrastat improved outcomes for people with unstable angina, whether or not they have to go on to have procedures to improve blood flow to the heart," said PRISM study leader Dr. Harvey White of Green Lane Hospital in New Zealand.
